name: Iris Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Greenmoor Wholesale, which supplies garden centres and pet shops across the region. Bird seed, compost, dog food, hosepipes, the whole lot. It's very seasonal, so from February to May I'm buying like mad, and the rest of the year I'm trying not to be left with a warehouse of compost. I use AI every day, mostly to match orders to the weather forecast, because one wet April can wreck a whole season. I love that part, getting the bet right. The tiring part is suppliers who promise March and deliver June.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jonas, who's a self-employed carpenter, mostly kitchens and staircases. We rent a terraced house near the canal. My pay's on the low side for buyers and Jonas's work goes up and down, so we've got maybe three weeks of money saved at any time. There aren't many buying jobs round here, so Greenmoor matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: handy, not magic. At work I'd keep sharing the weather trick with the other buyers. Online I'd post something practical, like how I use it, rather than a big opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau suits my job fine, but it doesn't fix our money. Jonas had two empty weeks in September and we went through most of our savings. My pay won't jump because AI stays ordinary. So it's the same tight life we've got now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and push Greenmoor to let me run the forecasting for all the buyers, not just my range. I'd ask for a small rise when I do. And Jonas and I would try to keep one month of rent in a separate account we don't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little itch that nothing's going to get easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jonas had two empty weeks. How does his work affect your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's feast or famine. One month he's got three kitchens booked, the next he's ringing round for small jobs. My salary is the steady bit of our household, which is funny because it's the low bit. So if anything happened to my job, we'd feel it the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager say if you asked to run the forecasting for everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen, my manager, would probably say yes but not pay me more. She's fair, but the budget's tight since the big garden chain started buying direct from factories. I'd do it anyway, because it makes me harder to let go.

I'd post **practical tips** rather than big opinions.
I'd keep sharing the **weather trick** with the other buyers at work.

Ask for a **small rise** when she does.
Keep one month of rent in a **separate account**.

steps.text: Offer to run weather-based forecasting for all Greenmoor buyers
Keep one month of rent in an untouched account
Keep buying the garden range through the spring rush

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so firms and staff should plan it together. At work I'd volunteer to lead the change. With friends I'd say buying will look very different in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Greenmoor would want one buyer running the system instead of four buyers doing it by hand. I'd want to be that one, and I think I've got a decent shot. But a decent shot isn't safe, and if I miss, there's nothing similar round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a proper automated reorder setup for my range and show Helen the numbers within three months. I'd ask to be trained on whatever the company buys, first in line. And on the side I'd start doing Jonas's quotes and ordering with AI, so his business runs smoother whatever happens to mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A buzz and a knot together. I like the challenge but I know what's at stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you become the one buyer, what happens to the other three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't like. Paul's been there twenty years and he's lovely, but he still prints everything. I'd want the other buyers moved to supplier visits or quality checks, not just let go, but I don't decide. I'd still say that to Helen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned there's nothing similar nearby. Would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easily. Jonas's customers are all local, it's word of mouth. Moving would mean him starting from scratch. So I'd rather fight to stay the one buyer than move for another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need help for people fast, because two years is nothing. At work I'd be honest that buying as a job is probably finished. Online I'd probably share what I was doing, in case it helps someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my buying job's gone by 2028, even being good with the tools, because AGI doesn't need someone like me running it. The interesting thing is Jonas. Carpentry is hands-on, so he gets until about 2031, maybe longer for fiddly old staircases. So his business becomes our main income, which flips everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start working with Jonas now, part-time, doing his quoting, ordering and customer emails with AI, so he can take more jobs. I'd learn to do the basic labouring too, sanding and fitting. We'd cut everything non-essential and try to save two months before my job ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken, but with a plan I half believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only half believe it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Jonas's work depends on people having money to spend on kitchens. If loads of office jobs go in 2028, who's buying a new staircase? We'd be the last ones standing in a shrinking market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas when you suggest working together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you're the business now and I'm the office. He'd be pleased and nervous, because he likes working alone. We'd argue about how he prices jobs, I already know that.

I'd admit at work that buying as a job is **probably finished**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a smart switch, so start now. At work I'd tell people to pick what they'll do next while they still have a salary. I'd write about it online, practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me about four as a buyer, which is a lot of salary to save from. Then Jonas and I would run the business properly, maybe doing fitted kitchens with a small team. He'd have until about 2034 on the tools. It's still an end date, but it's a real stretch of life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Greenmoor and become the person running their AI ordering. Evenings I'd set up proper systems for Jonas's business: booking, quoting, invoicing. And we'd put aside a hundred and fifty a month towards a van and tools for when we expand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly purposeful. A bit of worry, but more energy than dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good day look like in 2030, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me at Greenmoor in the morning checking the AI's orders, then out to a customer's house in the afternoon measuring up a kitchen with Jonas. Home by six. Honestly, that sounds better than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying there's an end date. What happens after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. Maybe people still want a human to design their kitchen, maybe not. I'd rather plan for five good years than freeze because I can't see fifteen.

I'd tell people to choose their next step while they **still have a salary**.
think: I'd get about **four years** of buyer's salary to save from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and I'd tell people to treat it like one. At work I'd keep leading on the tools. Online I'd be the optimist in the comments, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means my job's probably safe for a good while, and I'd likely move up as the AI person. Jonas's business could grow slowly with my help. By the mid-2030s I'd want us to own something, maybe the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to automate most of the reordering at Greenmoor over the next two years and take on a bigger role. We'd save steadily, then put money into a small workshop unit for Jonas within five years. And I'd keep doing his admin on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. The usual money worry, but no fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound much calmer here. Is that real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Three weeks of savings is still three weeks of savings, whatever happens with AI. If Jonas's van broke tomorrow, AGI in 2036 would be the last thing on my mind. But for the work itself, yes, I feel fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any change to your plans at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably think about kids around thirty-two, once the workshop is sorted. In the fast pictures I wouldn't even think about it. Ten years makes it feel possible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd be relying on Jonas's business just as people stop spending. What would help is support for small trades businesses, like cheap loans or grants for tools. And some kind of income floor while households switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this depends on the person you live with. My plans all lean on Jonas being hands-on. If my partner were an accountant instead of a carpenter, I'd be telling you a very different story.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: If my partner were an accountant instead of a carpenter, I'd be telling you a very different story.
portrait: Iris is a 27-year-old buyer of **garden and pet supplies** who uses AI daily to match orders to the weather.
She rents with her partner Jonas, a **self-employed carpenter**, and they keep about three weeks of money.
She'd move **first** in every picture, automating her own range to stay the one buyer left.
In the AGI pictures she plans around **his hands-on work**, which gets three extra years.
Her mood stays **uneasy to alarmed**, eased by long warnings but held back by thin savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the household would rely on his trade just as customers stop spending.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans or grants** for small trades businesses.
